title: Chapter 78 — Cistern and Buckets
paragraphs: Nimble as a cat, Tashtego climbs aloft and, without changing his upright posture, runs straight out along the overhanging main-yard-arm to the point where it projects exactly over the hoisted Tun. He has taken with him a light tackle called a whip, consisting of only two parts running through a single-sheaved block (a pulley with a single wheel). Securing this block so that it hangs down from the yard-arm, he swings one end of the rope until it is caught and firmly held by a hand on deck. Then, hand over hand, down the other part, the Indian drops through the air until he deftly lands on the summit of the head. There — still raised high above the rest of the company, to whom he calls out in lively fashion — he seems some Turkish Muezzin calling the good people to prayer from the top of a tower. A short-handled sharp spade is sent up to him, and he diligently searches for the proper place to begin breaking into the Tun. In this business he goes very carefully, like a treasure-hunter in some old house, sounding the walls to find where the gold is walled in. By the time this cautious search is over, a stout iron-bound bucket, exactly like a well-bucket, has been attached to one end of the whip, while the other end, stretched across the deck, is held there by two or three alert hands. These now hoist the bucket within reach of the Indian, to whom someone else has handed up a very long pole. Inserting this pole into the bucket, Tashtego guides the bucket down into the Tun until it entirely disappears; then, when he gives the word to the seamen at the whip, up comes the bucket again, all bubbling like a dairymaid's pail of new milk. Carefully lowered from its height, the brimming bucket is caught by a hand appointed for the purpose and quickly emptied into a large tub. Then it goes back up aloft and through the same round again, until the deep cistern will yield no more. Toward the end, Tashtego has to ram his long pole harder and harder, and deeper and deeper into the Tun, until some twenty feet of the pole have gone down.

Now, the people of the Pequod had been baling for some time in this way, and several tubs had been filled with the fragrant sperm, when all at once a strange accident happened. Whether it was that Tashtego, that wild Indian, was so heedless and reckless as to let go for a moment his one-handed hold on the great cabled tackles holding up the head; or whether the place where he stood was so treacherous and oozy; or whether the Evil One himself would have it happen so, without stating his particular reasons — how exactly it was, there is no telling now; but suddenly, as the eightieth or ninetieth bucket came suckingly up — my God! poor Tashtego — like the twin bucket that goes down as the other comes up in a real well, dropped head first down into this great Tun of Heidelburgh, and with a horrible oily gurgling went clean out of sight!

"Man overboard!" cried Daggoo, who, amid the general dismay, was the first to come to his senses. "Swing the bucket this way!" And he put one foot into it, the better to secure his slippery handhold on the whip itself, and the hoisters ran him high up to the top of the head, almost before Tashtego could have reached its bottom inside. Meanwhile, there was a terrible tumult. Looking over the side, they saw the head, lifeless until then, throbbing and heaving just below the surface of the sea, as if at that moment seized by some momentous idea; whereas it was only the poor Indian unconsciously revealing by those struggles the perilous depth to which he had sunk.

At this instant, while Daggoo, on the summit of the head, was clearing the whip — which had somehow got fouled in the great cutting tackles — a sharp cracking noise was heard; and to the unspeakable horror of all, one of the two enormous hooks holding up the head tore out, and with a vast vibration the enormous mass swung sideways, until the drunken ship reeled and shook as if struck by an iceberg. The one remaining hook, on which the entire strain now depended, seemed every instant on the point of giving way — an event made still more likely by the violent motions of the head.

"Come down, come down!" yelled the seamen to Daggoo. But with one hand holding on to the heavy tackles, so that if the head should drop he would still remain suspended, the negro, having cleared the foul line, rammed the bucket down into the now collapsed well, meaning that the buried harpooner should grasp it and so be hauled out.
"In heaven's name, man," cried Stubb, "are you ramming home a cartridge there? — Stop! How will that help him — jamming that iron-bound bucket on top of his head? Stop, will you!"
"Stand clear of the tackle!" cried a voice like the bursting of a rocket.

Almost in the same instant, with a thunder-boom, the enormous mass dropped into the sea, like Niagara's Table Rock into the whirlpool; the suddenly relieved hull rolled away from it so far that the glittering copper sheathing far down her side came into view; and all caught their breath as Daggoo, half swinging — now over the sailors' heads, and now over the water — was dimly seen through a thick mist of spray, clinging to the dangling tackles, while poor, buried-alive Tashtego was sinking utterly down to the bottom of the sea! But hardly had the blinding vapor cleared away when a naked figure with a boarding-sword in his hand was seen for one swift moment hovering over the bulwarks. The next, a loud splash announced that my brave Queequeg had dived to the rescue. Everyone rushed together to the side, and every eye counted every ripple, as moment followed moment and no sign of either the sinker or the diver could be seen. Some hands now jumped into a boat alongside and pushed a little way off from the ship.

"Ha! Ha!" cried Daggoo all at once, from his now quiet, swinging perch overhead. And looking further off from the side, we saw an arm thrust upright from the blue waves — a sight as strange as an arm thrust forth from the grass over a grave.

"Both! Both! — it is both!" cried Daggoo again with a joyful shout. And soon after, Queequeg was seen boldly striking out with one hand, and with the other clutching the long hair of the Indian. Drawn into the waiting boat, they were quickly brought to the deck. But Tashtego was long in coming to, and Queequeg did not look very well either.

Now, how had this noble rescue been accomplished? Why, diving after the slowly descending head, Queequeg, with his keen sword, had made side lunges near its bottom, so as to cut a large hole there; then, dropping his sword, he had thrust his long arm far inward and upward, and so hauled out poor Tash by the head. He declared that when he first reached in for him, a leg was presented; but, knowing well that that was not as it ought to be, and might cause great trouble, he had thrust back the leg, and by a deft heave and toss had turned the Indian a somersault; so that at the next try he came out in the good old way — head first. As for the great head itself, that was doing as well as could be expected.

And so, thanks to Queequeg's courage and great skill in obstetrics, the deliverance — or rather, the delivery — of Tashtego was successfully carried out, and in the face of the most awkward and seemingly hopeless obstacles, too. It is a lesson not to be forgotten. Midwifery should be taught alongside fencing and boxing, riding and rowing.

I know that this strange adventure of the Gay Header's will be sure to seem incredible to some landsmen, though they themselves may have seen or heard of someone falling into a cistern ashore — an accident which happens not infrequently, and with much less reason, too, than the Indian's, considering the extreme slipperiness of the rim of the Sperm Whale's well.

But perhaps it may be shrewdly objected: how is this? We thought the tissued, infiltrated head of the Sperm Whale was the lightest and most corklike part of him; and yet you make it sink in an element of far greater specific gravity than itself. We have you there. Not at all — I have you; for at the time poor Tash fell in, the case had been nearly emptied of its lighter contents, leaving little but the dense tendinous wall of the well — a double-welded, hammered substance, as I have said before, much heavier than sea water, a lump of which sinks in it almost like lead. But in this instance the tendency of this substance to sink rapidly was materially counteracted by the other parts of the head that remained attached to it, so that it sank very slowly and deliberately indeed, giving Queequeg a fair chance to perform his agile obstetrics on the run, as you might say. Yes, it was a running delivery, so it was.

Now, had Tashtego perished in that head, it would have been a very precious perishing: smothered in the very whitest and daintiest of fragrant spermaceti; coffined, hearsed and entombed in the secret inner chamber and sanctum sanctorum of the whale. Only one sweeter end comes readily to mind — the delicious death of an Ohio honey-hunter, who, seeking honey in the fork of a hollow tree, found such a great store of it that, as he leaned too far over, it sucked him in, so that he died embalmed. How many, do you think, have likewise fallen into Plato's honey head, and sweetly perished there?
